texts.full_text: in my package.json? - bytearcher http://bytearcher.com/articles/semver-explained-why-theres-a-caret-in-my-package-json/ ====== lemevi I've seen those characters in package.json but I never really bothered to look up how they worked, but now I will use them. Great article. I wonder though why they didn't go with using asterisk instead? Like say you used 1. * as the version specifier for a dependency - this would mean any major or minor updates are allowed. Using ^ is actually quite specific and tells npm (Node Package Manager) to only allow patch-level upgrades, ignoring those that change anything but the last number in your semver string. So with 1.*, you'd be allowing all versions starting from 0.9.99 up until a major version update happens. The caret (^), therefore helps ensure stability by restricting how far npm will go when resolving dependencies or updating packages. This is particularly useful for libraries that are frequently updated and may have breaking changes in minor releases, but generally provide backward compatibility with patch updates (fixes to bugs without changing the API). In summary: - Use 1.* if you want any version of package which has major versions more than your specified one. - Use ^1.2 for getting all patches i.e., only bug fixes or improvements within minor version. For a better understanding, this is what semver.org says about these two characters: "^X.Y.Z (caret) Matches any version that starts with the given X.Y but where Z may be replaced by anything including an empty string." IP sticks a protocol number into the right argument in a function call, and out pops a pointer to a function to pass the packet to for that process (or more likely a pointer to a work queue that process monitors). In the case of EIGRP, it's a work queue, and the process that monitors it is the EIGRP transport process (you should see a separate process for EIGRP and EIGRP transport in the processes running on a cisco box). Once this transport process is handed a slice of CPU, and it pulls a packet off the work queue. If there are several EIGRP processes running on the box, which one does it hand the packet to? It treats the AS number in the packet as a selector, just like TCP treats the socket as a selector among the various processes consuming packets (HTTP/80, ident, FTP, etc).
